The pressure to make up for these shortfalls is pushing institutional investors into a race to find yield that is increasingly taking them out of developed markets and deep into the emerging markets jungle.

This is not a new trend, but rather a continuation of the search for yield that started with the financial crisis. At that time, yields were low in developed markets but still higher than those in emerging markets, and the latter were also offering higher growth rates than the former. However, over the past seven years, the yield gap has narrow significantly. YTW spreads between developed and emerging bond markets have narrowed from 234 basis points in 2Q08 to 64bp in 2Q15, according to Barings.

This narrowing of the yield gap has increased the risk/return ratio for investors in developed markets. In the past, a typical conservative investor could find a higher return on a bond with a lower credit risk in emerging markets than on a bond of equal credit quality in developed markets. Today, with the narrowing of the yield gap, the risk/return ratio has changed, and investors in developed markets are now faced with the prospect of a lower return on bonds of equal credit quality in developed markets than they would receive from emerging market bonds of the same credit quality. In other words, the only way that conservative investors can generate the returns they need to cover their liabilities is to take on higher credit risk.

In the wild, Diascia personata forms a rosetting clump, but in our gardens it will produce numerous stems if it is cut back after the first flush of flowers. I have it growing in my gravel garden where it is in the full sun and in well-drained soil.

It is a very useful plant for the front of a gravel garden, but as it is quite stiff, it will also make a good statement plant in a container. If you grow it in a container, make sure you use a loam-based compot with added grit to ensure good drainage. It is a long-flowering plant, but if you want to extend the flowering season, you can take cuttings from non-flowering stems in the autumn.

Diascia personata is not widely available in garden centres but you can order it from specialist nurseries such as Hardy's Cottage Garden Plants in Norwich. It is a real find for the gravel gardening enthusiast.

## 3 The Effects Of Aging On Hair

Aging affects the hair in two main ways. The first is due to a reduction in the rate of cell division in the bulb at its base. This is the growing point of the hair, and the bulb is fed from the blood vessels that run through the scalp. As we age, these vessels become less effective and the rate of cell division slows, resulting in slower hair growth.

Secondly, the rate of hair loss also increases with age. The reason for this is not entirely clear, but it may be related to the thinning of the walls of the hair follicle, which increases the vulnerability of the hair follicle to damage.

The result of this combination of factors is a progressive loss of hair density, with the hair becoming finer and thinner, and a gradual increase in the extent of baldness. The hairline may recede, the temples may become thinner and eventually the bald patch may coalesce into a large area of baldness.

## 2 Genetic Hair Loss

The vast preponderance (95 per cent) of hair loss in men is due to a condition known as androgenetic alopecia, or male-pattern baldness.

Androgenetic alopcia is a genetic condition that affects the hair in the scalp. It is characterized by the gradual thinning of hair in a pattern that is characteristic for the condition.

In male-pattern baldness, the hair becomes progressively thinner and finer over the top of head, and the hairline receding at the temples and frontal region of the scalp. Eventually, the hair may become so thin that it disappears, leaving a bald patch on the top of the head.

Greg Gianforte, a tech entrepreneur and former state lawmaker, is pinning his third campaign in two years on Montana residents being better off economically since President Donald Trump took office and that the Republican voters will give him some of that credit as he seeks his first full-term in Montana's only House seat. Gianforte has tied his political fortunes to Trump as he seeks his first full term in Montana's only House seat. He won a May special election last year to serve the remainder of Ryan

Zinke's term after Zinke resigned to become Interior Department secretary. Gianforte has had to fend off renewed criticism over his assault of Guardian reporter Ben Jacobs the

day before the 2017 special election, and the Democratic nominee is running on the promise of universal health care and protection for the Affordable Care Act.

The two candidates are campaigning in a district that Trump won by 20 points in 2016, and the winner of the Nov. 8 election will likely have a solid

hold on that seat for years to come.
